title: The Career Skill Nobody Teaches: Communicating So People Listen
excerpt: Employers keep ranking communication above technical skills, yet nobody formally teaches it. True stories and practical habits for writing emails that get answered, speaking up in meetings, presenting to busy people, and handling feedback like a professional.
content:
Tunde was the sharpest analyst at a fintech in Lagos. His models were clean, his numbers were right, and everyone knew it. So when a team lead role opened up, he assumed it was his. It went to Amara instead. Her analysis was good, not brilliant. But her emails got answered the same day. Her update in the Monday meeting took ninety seconds and left nobody confused. When the commercial team needed the data story told without jargon, they asked for her by name. Tunde's manager put it plainly when Tunde asked why he had been passed over: "Your work is excellent. But half the time I can't tell what you're asking me for, and I can't put someone in front of clients if I have to translate them."

That sentence stung, and it should sting the rest of us a little too. School taught you to write essays and pass exams. Almost nobody taught you to write an email a busy person will act on, to make one clear point in a room full of seniors, or to receive criticism without shrinking. Yet from Lagos to Nairobi to Johannesburg, these are the skills that quietly decide who gets trusted, promoted, and remembered.

The evidence is not subtle

If that sounds like soft advice, look at the hiring data. When LinkedIn analysed what companies were actually recruiting for, communication came out as the single most in-demand skill of 2024, ahead of every technical skill on the list. Surveys of graduate recruiters repeat the message: in NACE's Job Outlook 2025 survey, written communication mattered to at least 70 percent of employers reviewing student CVs, and more than two thirds wanted strong verbal skills. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 places leadership and social influence among the core skills employers expect to matter most through 2030, right alongside analytical thinking and technology. And getting it wrong is counted in hard currency: research by Grammarly and The Harris Poll put the drain from poor workplace communication at an estimated 1.2 trillion dollars a year for US businesses, roughly 12,506 dollars per employee. Employers are not being sentimental when they rank communication first. They are counting.

Write emails a busy person can act on

Start with the medium you use most. Nobody watches you think; they read what you send. And most workplace email fails the same way: the request is buried in paragraph four, the subject line just says "Update", and the reader is left to work out what is being asked of them. Busy people do not do that work. They skim, move on, and your request dies quietly in an inbox.

The fix is almost mechanical. Put the ask in the first two lines: what you need, from whom, by when. Make the subject line do real work, because "Approval needed by Thursday: vendor contract" beats "Contract" every time. Keep one email to one request. Close by saying what happens next. Then read the draft aloud once and cut a third of it. Your reader will feel the difference immediately.

Speak so the meeting remembers you

Efua joined a consultancy in Accra straight out of university and spent her first months saying nothing in meetings. She had opinions. She also had a fear that whatever she said would sound junior. But her silence was read as absence, not caution, and after four months she realised the partners could barely place her name.

What changed was preparation, not confidence. Before each meeting she prepared one contribution: a question, a risk nobody had raised, or a short summary of where the discussion stood. She made herself speak within the first ten minutes, because the longer you wait, the heavier the silence gets. Within a few months, one partner had started turning to her to ask, "Efua, what are we missing?" Nobody hands you a voice in the room. You build it, one prepared sentence at a time.

Present the decision, not the slides

Presenting is the same skill standing up. A young engineer I met in Johannesburg lost an executive audience in minutes by walking them through forty slides of methodology before revealing what she actually wanted. Executives listen the other way round. Open with the problem, give your finding, and name the decision you need from them, all inside the first two minutes. Then show your evidence for as long as they will let you. The slides are an appendix to your point. They are not the point.

Feedback is a two-way skill

Then there is feedback, the conversation most of us dodge in both directions. Giving it well follows a learnable pattern: describe the specific behaviour, explain its impact, make a request. "When the report came in on Friday instead of Wednesday, I had no time to review it before the client call. Can we agree on Wednesday next time?" is respectful, clear, and hard to argue with. Vague criticism wrapped in politeness helps nobody.

Receiving feedback is harder and worth more. Say thank you before you say anything else. Ask one clarifying question instead of mounting a defence. Then act on what you heard, visibly. That habit will serve you from your first 90 days in a new job all the way to the corner office.

Habits that build the muscle

None of this requires talent. It requires practice, which is better news. Six habits worth starting this week:

  • Write the ask first. Draft every email by writing the request line before anything else, then build around it.
  • Prepare one contribution per meeting. A good question counts. Silence costs more than an imperfect comment.
  • Summarise out loud. Once a week, close a discussion by restating what was decided and who owes what. People will start assuming you lead things.
  • Read your writing aloud before sending. Your ear catches what your eye forgives.
  • Ask for feedback monthly. One question is enough: what should I do differently next month?
  • Explain your work to a non-expert. If you can make your aunt understand your job, you can make an executive understand your proposal.

Phrases that work

Because the hardest part is often finding the words in the moment, here are lines that earn their keep:

  • "Here is what I need from you, and by when." The opening of an email that gets answered.
  • "Can I check my understanding? I think we've agreed on X, and Y is still open." The summary move. It sounds senior because it is what senior people do.
  • "I see it differently, and here's why." Disagreement without apology and without attack.
  • "I don't know, and I'll find out by tomorrow." More credible than a shaky guess, every single time.
  • "What would make this a yes for you?" Turns a stalled request into a negotiation.
  • "Thank you, that's useful. Could you give me an example?" The feedback receiver's best friend.

The skill that improves every other skill

Tunde is fine, by the way. The rejection sent him back to his manager to ask exactly what unclear looked like, and he treated the answer as data rather than insult. He rewrote how he emailed, rehearsed his meeting updates, volunteered to present. Eighteen months later he leads a team of five, and colleagues describe him as the one who explains things properly. The models were never the problem.

Communication is the rare skill that upgrades every other skill you own. It is what turns an interview into a conversation instead of an interrogation, and it is why some people's names travel through networks that surface opportunities long before any job board: people can only recommend what they can repeat. Your technical ability got you into the room. How you communicate decides what happens once you are in it.
